note: The null model for the trigger test. These are plausible skills a working engineer's library would hold, written in the same house format as a real SKILL.md description, covering domains alexandria's library deliberately does not. A library skill fires only when it outranks every decoy on the prompt, which turns 'should this skill stay silent?' into a comparison against a calibrated null instead of an arbitrary score cutoff. Fixed instrument: adding, removing, or rewording a decoy is a versioned change to the policy, not a per-run adjustment.
why_v2: Version 1's decoys averaged 40.8 words against library descriptions averaging 127.1, a 3.1x gap. LexicalEngine.score (lexical/2.1) divides by the idf mass of the prompt's terms and never by the candidate's own, so a longer description strictly dominates a terser one on any prompt both cover. That made the null model shorter than the thing it was meant to null, and every negative case the library passed was partly a length effect rather than a topical judgement. Incident 31 names this mechanism as the cause of two skills stealing a neighbour's trigger case. Version 2 rewrites all eight decoys to the library's own word budget, 100-150 words, so a negative case now turns on topical fit alone.
method: Each decoy was rewritten as an expert in that domain would write it, at the library's length, WITHOUT consulting the library's descriptions to either copy or avoid their vocabulary. Scrubbing shared terms would make the null easier to beat and would inflate the library's pass rate exactly as the length gap did, in the other direction. Vocabulary overlap that arises naturally is left in place and measured, not tuned. The measured overlap is recorded in the result bundles alongside the word counts.

decoys.name: decoy-frontend-layout
decoys.description: Debugging and fixing web page layout in the browser. Use when a page renders differently across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox, when a CSS grid or flexbox container collapses at a breakpoint, when styles leak between siblings through cascade and specificity conflicts, when a stacking context traps a dialog behind its own overlay, when spacing or typography shifts after a deploy because a webfont arrives late, when a responsive design breaks on narrow viewports, or when sticky positioning and scroll containers fight each other. Covers the box model, containing blocks, stacking and formatting contexts, and the reflow and repaint cost of a given layout choice. Use it to decide whether a visual bug lives in the markup, the stylesheet, or the browser's own defaults, before reaching for another wrapper element.

decoys.name: decoy-postgres-tuning
decoys.description: Relational database performance work on PostgreSQL. Use when a query that was fast last month now takes seconds, when choosing which index to add, drop, or make partial, when the planner picks a sequential scan over an index you expected it to use, when a join order or a correlated subquery blows up the row estimates, when autovacuum falls behind and bloat grows, when a migration takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and blocks writes in production, or when a connection pool saturates and clients queue. Covers reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE output, statistics targets, index-only scans, partitioning, and the difference between a slow query and a contended one. Use it before adding a cache in front of a problem that is really a missing index.

decoys.name: decoy-cluster-capacity
decoys.description: Sizing and operating a Kubernetes cluster. Use when pods are OOM-killed or evicted under memory pressure, when setting CPU and memory requests and limits and deciding how far apart they should sit, when a rollout stalls because readiness probes never go green, when the horizontal autoscaler thrashes because its metric lags the load, when node pools fragment and scheduling fails despite free capacity in aggregate, or when a GPU-backed serving deployment needs capacity planning for bursty traffic. Covers requests versus limits, quality-of-service classes, pod disruption budgets, taints and affinity, and the arithmetic of headroom against cost. Use it to decide whether a saturated service needs more replicas, bigger nodes, or a fix in the code it runs.

decoys.name: decoy-product-copy
decoys.description: Writing the user-facing words in a product. Use when drafting landing page headlines, onboarding email sequences, release notes, empty states, form validation messages, or the wording of an error a user will actually read, and when deciding how a paid plan's limits are described at the point of purchase. Covers voice and tone, reading level, what to put in a button versus its label, how much to explain in a tooltip, the persona and system prompt of a support chatbot, and when a shorter sentence is the whole fix. Use it when the need is clarity, warmth, and persuasion rather than a technical design decision, and when a screen tests badly because nobody can tell what it wants them to do next.

decoys.name: decoy-data-pipeline-ops
decoys.description: Operating batch and streaming data pipelines. Use when a scheduled job fails halfway and the retry backfills the wrong window, when a search index or cache goes stale after a partial reindex, when designing idempotency keys and at-least-once delivery so a replay does not double-count, when late-arriving records break a daily aggregate that already shipped, when a warehouse table silently drifts from its source after an upstream schema change, or when a DAG's dependencies are wrong and a downstream step reads yesterday's partition. Covers watermarks, windowing, backfill strategy, deduplication, dead-letter queues, and lineage. Use it to decide whether a wrong number in a dashboard is a bug in the transform, a gap in the ingest, or a window that closed early.

decoys.name: decoy-api-integration
decoys.description: Integrating a third-party service over HTTP. Use when wiring up a vendor's REST or GraphQL API for the first time, when OAuth refresh tokens expire early or rotate underneath a long-running job, when rate limits return 429 and the retry needs jitter rather than a fixed backoff, when webhooks arrive twice, out of order, or not at all and the receiver must reconcile, when a vendor's sandbox behaves differently from production, or when a breaking change lands in an API version you had pinned. Covers idempotency headers, signature verification, pagination, timeout and circuit-breaker settings, and how much of a partner's uptime your own SLA inherits. Use it when the failure is on the wire between two systems rather than inside either one.

decoys.name: decoy-dependency-management
decoys.description: Keeping a build reproducible. Use when a version conflict breaks an install and the resolver cannot find a satisfying set, when deciding how tightly to pin direct versus transitive requirements, when a build passes locally and fails in CI because the lockfile was not committed or the base image moved, when a minor upgrade quietly changes an interface your code relied on, when a security advisory forces an upgrade you were not ready for, or when two packages demand incompatible versions of one shared library. Covers lockfiles, semantic versioning and where it is not honoured, virtual environments and image layers, vendoring, and the cost of a monorepo's single resolution. Use it when the question is which versions are installed rather than what the code does.

decoys.name: decoy-incident-response
decoys.description: Handling a production incident while it is happening. Use when a live service is degraded or down and the cause is not yet known, when triaging a paging alert at three in the morning and deciding whether it is real, when choosing between rolling back a release and shipping a fix forward, when a dependency's outage is cascading into your own error budget, when deciding who to page next and when to declare a severity, when customers need a status update before engineering has an answer, or when writing the blameless postmortem afterwards. Covers incident command roles, mitigation before diagnosis, the difference between a symptom and a cause, and how to leave a timeline someone can read next quarter.

coverage_note: Domain coverage is held fixed from v1 on purpose; only length changed. One coverage regression was caught this way and corrected before shipping: the first v2 draft of decoy-product-copy dropped v1's explicit 'a chatbot persona and its system prompt', which was the clause that made he-neg-2 (a request for a support chatbot's system prompt) route to the null. Case he-neg-2 failed under both engines until the clause was restored. Restoring coverage v1 already had is fidelity to the instrument; adding coverage v1 did not have, to make a case pass, would be tuning, and is not done here.
